theory.overview: Sorting is the process of arranging data in a particular order (ascending or descending). It's fundamental to many algorithms and enables efficient searching. Key algorithms include Quick Sort (average O(n log n)), Merge Sort (stable O(n log n)), Heap Sort (in-place O(n log n)), and specialized algorithms like Counting Sort and Radix Sort for integer data. Understanding sorting tradeoffs helps select the right algorithm for specific constraints.

keyConcepts.name: Comparison Sorts
keyConcepts.description: Algorithms like Quick Sort, Merge Sort, Heap Sort that compare elements. Lower bound is O(n log n) comparisons.

keyConcepts.name: Linear Time Sorts
keyConcepts.description: Counting Sort, Radix Sort, Bucket Sort achieve O(n) by exploiting data properties, not comparing.

keyConcepts.name: Stability
keyConcepts.description: Stable sorts preserve relative order of equal elements. Important when sorting by multiple keys.

keyConcepts.name: In-Place vs Out-of-Place
keyConcepts.description: In-place uses O(1) extra space (Quick Sort). Out-of-place needs more space (Merge Sort with O(n)).

complexity.quickSort: O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst
complexity.mergeSort: O(n log n) always, O(n) space
complexity.heapSort: O(n log n) always, O(1) space
complexity.countingSort: O(n + k) where k is range
